patient_information: A 31-year-old man, diagnosed with HIV 6 years ago, who is not yet on antiretroviral therapy (ART) or co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. His CD4 count was 280/μL one month prior to presentation, and on admission was 150/μL with an HIV viral load of 1,500,000 copies/mL. He denies any recreational drug use and has never smoked tobacco. He has no other significant past medical history.
chief_complaint: A 6-week history of increasing shortness of breath on exertion, dry cough, and drenching night sweats.
history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 6-week history of progressively worsening shortness of breath on exertion, a dry cough, and drenching night sweats. He also reported general fatigue and a weight loss of about 10kg over the preceding 5 months.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a business traveller who travels extensively. In the past 6 months, he had work trips to Europe, China, Korea, Japan, Singapore, and the United States. He lives with his male partner.
vitals: On presentation, his temperature was 39.2°C (102.6°F), blood pressure was 120/70mmHg, pulse was 100 bpm, and respiratory rate was 26 breaths per minute. His oxygen saturation was 87% on ambient air, which improved to 97% on 15L of O2.
physical_exam: The patient was alert and able to complete full sentences, but was short of breath at rest. Auscultation of the chest was clear. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.
labs_and_diagnostics: Laboratory results showed a normal full blood count and normal renal and liver function tests. C-reactive protein was elevated at 6.7 mg/dL. Arterial blood gases on ambient air showed a pH of 7.44 and a PaO2 of 7.6 kPa, consistent with type 1 respiratory failure. His CD4 count was 150/μL. A chest radiograph showed bilateral perihilar infiltrates. A CT-pulmonary angiogram ruled out pulmonary embolism but revealed extensive “ground-glass” infiltrates in both lungs, especially in the lower lobes. Serum 1,3 β-D-glucan was markedly elevated at >500 pg/mL. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid analysis confirmed the diagnosis, with Grocott staining revealing Pneumocystis jirovecii cystic forms and a strongly positive PCR for P. jirovecii DNA.
differential_diagnosis: The primary differential diagnosis was Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), given the patient's presentation as an ART-naïve HIV-positive individual with a low CD4 count, progressive shortness of breath, and typical chest radiograph findings. Other considerations included tuberculosis, atypical bacterial pneumonia, cryptococcosis, or histoplasmosis. A CT pulmonary angiogram was performed to rule out pulmonary embolism.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was managed with high-flow oxygen, high-dose co-trimoxazole, and prednisolone. His tachycardia and hypoxia improved with treatment. Ten days into treatment, he commenced antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz. Two weeks into PCP treatment, he developed a pruritic maculopapular rash, leading to a change from co-trimoxazole to clindamycin and primaquine for the final week of his 21-day course, and his efavirenz was replaced. After completing treatment, he was started on dapsone and pyrimethamine for secondary prophylaxis.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is severe Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii. This was established in an ART-naïve HIV-positive patient with a low CD4 count (150/μL) presenting with classic subacute respiratory failure and hypoxia. The diagnosis was supported by imaging showing bilateral ground-glass infiltrates and a highly elevated serum β-glucan level (>500 pg/mL). It was definitively confirmed by bronchoalveolar lavage fluid analysis, which identified P. jirovecii cystic forms via Grocott staining and was strongly positive by PCR.
